audience: Corporate HSE, site leadership and the investigation team
status: Learning purposes: not a statutory document; draft: the investigation status is in progress

incident.title: Hazira gas terminal condensate release and fire

data_quality.text: Draft learnings from an unreviewed analysis: the ProbeMatrix investigation status is in progress and no finding is marked as edited by a person. Validate before adoption.
The export's Causal Chain sheet is empty. The links between codes are counted from the factor codes each finding names in its causal explanation (causal_graph.json).

bottom_line.text: The findings reach company management (level 3, 143 findings) and no higher: nothing in the export is placed at the regulator or government levels.
Technical and operational management (level 4) is the busiest level, with 166 findings.
The strongest links across levels run from missing policy and guidance at level 4 (SVI 1.4) down to checklists not followed at level 5 and unclear technical guidance at level 6: 6 mentions each.

items.text: Placements above the company level are inferred from codes and departments. A person confirms them before this map is shared.

sections.heading: Levels the export does not reach

items.text: Level 1 (Government policy and budgeting) and level 2 (Regulatory bodies and associations) have no placements. No finding is tagged to a regulator, and the default rules place nothing at government level. The nearest findings are at level 3: external-audit recommendations extended without the required approval. An empty level is a question for the organisation, not a finding that nobody there contributed.

items.lesson: The management-of-change procedure existed at company level but was not in use, so part and material substitutions reached the work site with no review.
items.explanation: Two company-level codes carry it down the map: OIC 2.1 links to routine violations at level 5 (5 mentions) and OIC 2.7 to misapplied procedures at level 5 (5 mentions). The procedure was published in 2016 and no change was put through it after 2018 [EVD-2986].

items.lesson: No procedure for calibrating high-pressure meters and returning them to service existed at the operational management level, so the work at the meter had no checklist or test to follow.
items.explanation: SVI 1.4 at level 4 links to checklists not followed at level 5 and to unclear technical guidance at level 6, 6 mentions each. The gasket was replaced and the meter returned to service with no test above operating pressure [EVD-2894].

items.lesson: Safety audits at company level used generic checklists, so assurance could not see plant-specific conditions at the work site.
items.explanation: OIC 2.7 at level 3 links to checklists not followed at level 5 (5 mentions), and supervisory oversight at level 4 (SVI 1.1) to the same code (6 mentions). The 2018 and 2019 internal audits kept no filled checklists [EVD-7681].

items.lesson: Company practice for known problems shaped the equipment level: repeat failures of the same seal stayed routine repairs, not a reliability warning.
items.explanation: OIC 2.1 at level 3 and maintenance at level 6 (PTE 2.12) both link to routine violations at level 5 (5 and 4 mentions). The seal was replaced three times in 22 months [EVD-1494].

items.lesson: The company's emergency plan named the major-leak scenario but gave no isolation criteria, and the gap carried through the operational guidance to the people responding.
items.explanation: OIC 2.1 and OIC 2.7 at level 3 each link to SVI 1.4 at level 4 (4 mentions each), and SVI 1.4 links to unclear technical guidance at level 6. The plan covered leaks but not isolation or stoppage [EVD-4052].

items.question: Is level 3 (company management) right for the 143 findings placed there, and which decisions were taken at corporate rather than at site level?
items.why: Level 3 is inferred: 134 findings come from HFACS level 4 codes and 9 from corporate and vendor tags, not from what the export says about who decided.
items.good_evidence: Corporate HSE standards, management committee minutes and the delegation of authority for maintenance and change

items.question: Should the seven vendor findings stay at level 3, including the lost P&ID drawing that the HFACS codes put at levels 2 and 3?
items.why: The vendor tag moves a finding to level 3 whatever its HFACS level, so these placements are inferred.
items.good_evidence: The vendor contract and the drawing approval record for the metering skid

items.question: Did the regulator's inspections, approvals or audit follow-up play a part at level 2 (regulatory bodies and associations)?
items.why: Level 2 is a gap: no finding is tagged to a regulator, so the map is empty there. The export also mentions regulator involvement while it records the incident as not reportable.
items.good_evidence: Statutory inspection and approval records for the terminal, and the regulator's correspondence on the external audit

items.question: Did any government policy or budget decision shape the conditions at level 1 (government policy and budgeting)?
items.why: Level 1 has no placement rule, so it stays empty unless the organisation adds what it knows.
items.good_evidence: Policy or budget documents the organisation names; they are outside this export
